lede: You asked whether anything else deserved a questionnaire and picked four; this one is mystery, horror and intrigue: the Lord of the Mysteries register and the Night Watch, fair clues, how secrets surface, horror pacing, court and faction intrigue, and lies that stay uncorrected. Three research passes (the house archive, the current law, and the traditions from Knox and Holmes to Junji Ito and le Carré) stand behind 46 questions in five sections, each with a recommendation you can take as it stands, and nothing the Style Law or the Combat Law settled is asked again: the settled list at the end says what was left alone and why. Answer the seven Keystones first, since most later questions lean on them.

question.title: True words that deceive
question.question: Does a true sentence built to deceive owe a tell, as a lie does?
question.context: R49-36: 'Every lie leaves a catchable tell'; nothing rules the literal truth built to mislead, intrigue's sharpest tool and Mantel's Cromwell's daily work. Hild names it in the archive: Edward's truth 'built to make me act, which is a third thing'. Samples: written scene, past tense; at a Kharven fire Arnbjorn asks after an old man's death, and Hrolf's answer is true.

options.label: Tell owed, as a lie
options.consequence: R49-36 extends to deceiving truths: the speaker shows a body tell, as a liar would.
options.sample: "I was at my own woodpile all that night," Hrolf said. "Ask anyone on the row." Arnbjorn did not need to ask. Half the row had heard the axe going till the small hours. He kept his eyes on the rider's breath-plume instead, and it came short and quick through the nose, the way a man breathes who has run up a slope, though Hrolf had been sitting at the fire since the skin went round. A full stack speaks louder than a full mouth. Hrolf's mouth was full tonight.

options.label: The fact is the tell
options.consequence: No body tell, since the speaker tells the truth; the deceit lives in what the sentence leaves out, and the page carries a fact that turns its meaning where a careful player can line it up. The notes name that fact.
options.sample: "I was at my own woodpile all that night," Hrolf said. "Ask anyone on the row." Arnbjorn did not need to ask. Half the row had heard the axe going till the small hours, and Hrolf's breath came easy, and his hands lay still on his knees. It stayed true until the boy who kept the horse lines said, later and to nobody in particular, that Hrolf had moved his stack in the autumn, round behind the old man's house, where the wind was better.

options.label: No tell owed
options.consequence: A deceiving truth owes nothing; the player must parse the words, and the sentence may mislead for good.
options.sample: "I was at my own woodpile all that night," Hrolf said. "Ask anyone on the row." Arnbjorn did not need to ask. Half the row had heard the axe going till the small hours. Hrolf's breath came easy and his hands lay still on his knees, and when the skin came round he drank and passed it on as a man does with nothing behind his teeth. Arnbjorn thanked him, struck him off the slate he kept in his head, and went to ask the next man.

question.rec_reason: A man telling the truth has nothing to sweat, so a body tell would be false to him; the fair catch is a fact on the record, the house's own clue bed, which keeps every deception findable as MY3's herrings and R71-84's forgeries already are.

question.title: The thing left unexplained
question.question: What does Table Rule 8's unexplained notice owe now, and does it still come every turn?
question.context: Table Rule 8: 'One thing per turn his PC notices and you don't explain.' Prose made the same quota optional (R49-11: 'no per-scene minimum'), and its ancestor R6-3 had each notice resolve later. The lie half of Rule 8 is the table questionnaire's WD6, and K3 sets when secrets pay. The Kharven oil lamp and burn-salve sit in no record.

options.label: Every turn, texture only
options.consequence: One a turn, as now; each is a world-only detail (R53-30) left unread that owes no payoff and is never a clue, so clues come only by a case's own roads.

options.label: Every turn, each a seed
options.consequence: One a turn; each is logged in MY2's records and pays under K3: Chekhov's gun (the playwright's rule that a thing shown must be used) applied to the iceberg.

options.label: Every turn, marked in notes
options.consequence: One a turn; the notes mark each as texture or seed, seeds logged in MY2's records to pay under K3 and texture never, and the page never says which.

options.label: When a scene has one
options.consequence: R49-11 carried to the table: no count; an unexplained notice comes when a scene has one worth leaving, marked texture or seed in the notes as in C.

question.rec_reason: It matches the prose law he ruled on 2026-09-26 (R49-11) and the table questionnaire's lean on Rule 8's lie half (WD6), ends the per-turn quota behind the archive's 'could make nothing of it' habit (ME3's B), and the notes still mark seed from texture, so every planted mystery is on record and can pay.

question.title: A rival on the case
question.question: When an NPC works the same case as Isaac's PC, may the NPC solve it?
question.context: R71-6 has Natalie place the tell and never draw his PC's conclusion, while Table Rule 3 has NPCs pursue their own wants, and a Watch Searcher (an investigator on the crown's warrant) such as Orin Farrant works cases of her own. R12-4 makes a confident wrong theory the kit's best tool. Hunter x Hunter's rival hunters race the hero to the prize.

options.label: Evidence only
options.consequence: An NPC beside his PC finds and hands over evidence as a bare fact (R6-2) and never says what it means; every conclusion is Isaac's to draw.

options.label: Theories, often wrong
options.consequence: NPCs voice their own theories in their own voices, confident and often wrong (R12-4); a right one is spoken only after his PC has held every clue it rests on.

options.label: A rival on his own clock
options.consequence: B, and an NPC on the same case runs it as a Front and may close it first, right or wrong, from clues the page has shown; a wrong close can hang an innocent, a right one takes the credit and the fee.

question.rec_reason: NPCs who want things pursue them (Table Rule 3) and the world moves without him (Rule 4); a rival who can win or blunder gives every case a clock and a cost, as MY4's misses do, and since he reasons only from what the page has shown, nothing is rigged (R57-10).

question.title: One man, two faces
question.question: When an NPC lives two lives (an alias, a cell name, a mask at a gathering), what must tie the faces together for a player to catch?
question.context: Lord of the Mysteries runs on layered identities: its hero presides over a gathering whose members know each other only by card names. WOTR has the pieces (The Mother's cultures go by chosen names; Malphas is filed by his title, R67-8; Wren wrote under a blank seal in a hand not his) but no rule for them. His PC's own identities stay Isaac's.

options.label: A habit carries over
options.consequence: The two faces share one tell (a hand, a habit, a smell, a turn of phrase), shown in each face before the unmasking, on R71-23's twice-shown rhythm.

options.label: The paper links them
options.consequence: The link lives in the record (a hand, a seal, a payment, a lodging), the house's clue bed; the body and the voice may be perfect.

options.label: Either road; masks leak
options.consequence: A or B, at least one link planted before the unmasking; a face held by a working has its Codex line and leaks a seam, as an impression-body (a dead man's likeness worked from his Trace) does under R71-87.

options.label: Nothing owed
options.consequence: A second identity may hold for good; its truth sits in MY2's file, and the world owes the player no link.

question.rec_reason: It takes the Lord of the Mysteries masks he picked on WOTR's fair-counter terms: a habit for the reader who watches people, a paper for the one who reads ledgers, and no working hides a face for free. D lets a disguise win with nothing to catch (R57-10).

rec_changes.rec_reason: It is R71-6's line moved from wounds to dread, agrees with R71-17's trained composure and with the table questionnaire's reflexes as world facts, and every sign has a cause in the room he can find and answer, which is his fair-counter rule; the fear itself stays his.

The seam is the intrigue form of a findable counter, and an NPC's record of what he knows of the PC keeps that NPC from acting on more than he could know (R48-36); B is the roster's half of K4's Ledger line on who knows he knows. C duplicates the Front's own numbered steps and the planted-sign list in the notes.

intros.MY: How a case is built, worked and closed: clue counts and records, false leads and the fail state, the Night Watch on the page, interrogation and true words that deceive, witnesses, instruments and the investigator's head, the lie never caught and the thing left unexplained, the solution and the reveal, and the Watch and its rivals at the table. MY16 to MY18 were added in the cross-check and sit beside the questions they answer.
intros.IN: How councils turn, how deep schemes nest, who may betray, how leverage and spies work, what ties one man's two faces together, how much of a Front (a faction's clock of moves) Isaac sees, and whether a court or a file can be bought. Interrogation and true words that deceive are asked under Mystery (MY6, MY16). In the samples a factor is a merchant's agent who buys on commission, and the Assistants are a livery company's governing court.

settled_extra.point: Every beat carries at least one detail that could only exist in this world, and in written scenes the not-knowing quotas (one thing the POV cannot interpret, one confident wrong inference) are optional, with no per-scene minimum.
settled_extra.why_not_asked: Live prose law; MY17 asks only what Table Rule 8's unexplained notice owes in a roleplay turn.
